item.title: JinkoSolar unveils 28%-efficient back-contact TOPCon solar cell with amorphous silicon HJT passivation
item.dc:creator: Vincent Shaw
item.description: JinkoSolar has unveiled its first back-contact solar cell technology, combining TOPCon and heterojunction passivation in a new architecture called TAC. The Chinese manufacturer reported a peak cell conversion efficiency of 28%.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese PV module maker JinkoSolar unveiled its TOPCon-based Amorphous-Si Passivating Cell (TAC) technology at its Global Tech Day event in Shanghai on Oct. 17. According to a technical white paper published by the company, the architecture combines TOPCon electron-selective contacts with heterojunction (HJT) hole-selective contacts and a rear-electrode layout.

The design uses an n-type crystalline silicon wafer with two alternating carrier-selective contact regions on the rear surface. Both positive and negative electrodes are located on the rear, eliminating front-side metallisation and the associated optical shading losses.

The electron-collecting n-type region retains the contact structure used in TOPCon cells, consisting of an approximately 1 nm to 2 nm silicon oxide tunneling layer and heavily doped polycrystalline silicon. This structure enables selective electron transport with low contact resistance while suppressing carrier recombination.

The hole-collecting p-type region uses intrinsic and doped hydrogenated amorphous silicon (a-Si), drawing on HJT cell technology. JinkoSolar said the configuration improves surface passivation and open-circuit voltage. A transparent conductive oxide (TCO) layer facilitates lateral carrier transport, while the amorphous silicon passivation process takes place at temperatures below 200 C.

High-precision laser patterning and dielectric isolation separate the two contact regions. JinkoSolar describes the architecture as a “2+1” design, combining TOPCon electron contacts, HJT hole contacts and a rear-electrode structure.

TAC belongs to the broader back-contact (BC) cell category, which includes architectures using different passivation and carrier-selective contact technologies. Unlike conventional front-contact TOPCon cells, TAC eliminates front-side metal contacts to reduce shading losses. Its distinguishing feature among BC technologies is the integration of TOPCon and amorphous silicon heterojunction contacts on the same wafer.

JinkoSolar has also developed a full-area passivation approach, called the Global Passivation Process (GPP), to reduce recombination losses across the contact regions. Another process, Multi-Dimensional Charge Passivation (MCP 2.0), targets carrier recombination at cut-cell edges. It uses a cut-before-passivation sequence, followed by chemical, field-effect and hydrogen passivation of the exposed surfaces.

Other cell-level features include high-purity, low-oxygen n-type silicon wafers and a light-trapping structure combining surface texturing, antireflection coatings and rear reflection. The white paper specifies a bulk minority-carrier lifetime exceeding 2 ms and a bulk recombination current density below 5 fA/cm² for the silicon substrate.

JinkoSolar said TAC production cell efficiency has exceeded 27%, with a peak efficiency of 28%. The company’s Oct. 17 announcement identifies the 28% figure as peak cell efficiency. However, the white paper does not specify a third-party certification, test area or average production-line efficiency for the result.

In its first-half 2026 financial report, JinkoSolar separately reported a third-party-certified conversion efficiency of 27.2% for an n-type BC research cell. The company, however, did not identify that result as a TAC measurement.

JinkoSolar identified low-temperature metallisation, copper-containing contact materials and the potential use of TAC as a bottom-cell platform for perovskite-silicon tandem devices as areas for further development.

From pv magazine Global

item.title: Leapting launches autonomous forklift for solar module transport
item.dc:creator: Lior Kahana
item.description: The Chinese robotics manufacturer has introduced an autonomous tracked forklift capable of transporting solar module pallets weighing up to 3,000 kg. The battery-powered machine features a maximum lifting height of three metres, a 30-degree climbing capability and a navigation system combining GNSS-RTK, laser SLAM and computer vision.
item.content:encoded:
China’s Leapting, a developer of robotic automation solutions for the PV industry, has unveiled a new autonomous forklift for utility-scale solar construction sites.

Dubbed Auto-Navigation Forklift Robot (AFR), the system can transport pallets of solar modules weighing up to 3,000 kg from laydown yards to installation rows without a human operator.

“The AFR combines GPS-RTK, laser-based simultaneous localisation and mapping (SLAM), and 3D computer vision to locate pallets, identify fork-hole coordinates in real time, and auto-plan insertion paths,” the company said in a statement. “It further features 360-degree multi-line LiDAR, intelligent obstacle avoidance, and a three-tier braking system.”

The navigation system combines high-precision GNSS-RTK positioning with SLAM for local perception and positioning corrections. According to the manufacturer, the system can identify pallet locations, orientation angles and the three-dimensional coordinates of fork openings in real time. It then automatically calculates insertion and extraction paths and adjusts the mast and forks for pallet handling.

The company said the system can also detect whether pallets contain materials and recognise common pallet standards, including European EUR/EPAL and Japanese JIS specifications.

The AFR measures 4.8 m × 1.8 m × 2.15 m and weighs 5,500 kg. It has a standard load centre distance of 600 mm and a maximum lifting height of three metres. Its two-stage, full-free-lift mast features laterally adjustable forks for precise pallet alignment, the company said.

The forklift uses a tracked chassis with two independently driven 4 kW motors. It reaches a maximum speed of 3 km/h when fully loaded and 4 km/h when unloaded, with adjustable driving speeds. Differential track steering allows the machine to rotate on the spot.

“High-strength engineering-grade steel tracks, with low ground contact pressure, are suitable for diverse complex road conditions and provide stable loads,” the company said.

According to the technical datasheet, the AFR can negotiate gradients of at least 30 degrees on hard surfaces and has a maximum wading depth of 0.3 m. It also supports a maximum forward inclination angle of 4 degrees and a maximum pitch angle of 11 degrees. The manufacturer said the machine is suitable for hard roads, desert terrain, gravel surfaces and lightly uneven or muddy ground.

The AFR is powered by a 48 V, 400 Ah lithium battery, providing a nominal energy capacity of 19.2 kWh and at least eight hours of operation under standard conditions. It supports automatic charging and manual fast charging, with AC 220 V and AC 380 V charging connections. In addition to fully autonomous operation, users can select semi-automatic or manual remote-control modes.

For safety, the forklift incorporates multi-line LiDAR sensors for 360-degree obstacle detection, along with audible and visual warnings. Its three-tier braking system combines electronic, mechanical and parking brakes. Emergency stop buttons are installed at several points on the vehicle exterior.

An integrated inertial measurement unit (IMU) continuously monitors the vehicle’s tilt angle and triggers an alarm and automatic stop if a preset threshold is exceeded.

The AFR offers an IP67 ingress protection rating, depending on the configuration. The company specifies an operating temperature range of -10 C to 50 C and a storage temperature range of -20 C to 60 C.

From pv magazine Global

item.title: Tender success creates pathway to progress up to 13 GW of renewables
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: The South Australian government has selected four proposed renewable energy projects with a combined generation capacity of almost 13 GW to progress near the industrial centre of Whyalla in the state’s Upper Spencer Gulf region.
item.content:encoded:
Four proposed solar, wind, and battery energy storage projects that would add a combined 12.66 GW of new generation capacity to the grid have been successful in the South Australian government’s competitive tender process for land released under the state’s renewable energy framework.

The successful proposals have now secured the right to apply for a renewable energy feasibility licence in the Whyalla West release area, part of more than 11,000 square kilometres of land opened by the state government earlier this year for the potential development of large-scale renewables projects.

The successful projects include a 4.7 GW wind and solar proposal from South Australia-based Altra Energy, a 360 MW solar proposal from French developer Neoen, and a 1.6 GW wind project proposed by Heron Energy. Australian developer Windlab has proposed the largest project, combining up to 6 GW of solar and wind energy generation. The project’s first stage is expected to comprise up to 1 GW of wind generation and battery energy storage.

South Australian Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis said the scale of the proposed developments represents one of the largest renewable energy opportunities released in the state, adding the projects could underpin the next era of green industrial growth in the Upper Spencer Gulf region.

“This is an extraordinary opportunity for Whyalla and the Upper Spencer Gulf, with almost 13 GW of proposed renewable energy generation that could help shape the region’s industrial future,” he said.

“For generations, Whyalla has been one of South Australia’s great industrial centres. We want to build on that strength, attracting new investment and creating opportunities for the next generation of industry.”

Koutsantonis acknowledged that all four projects are at an early stage, and that there is significant work ahead, but said their success in the tender process is an important step towards unlocking the region’s renewable energy potential.

The successful companies can now apply for renewable energy feasibility licences. These would allow developers to undertake detailed technical, commercial and environmental investigations. Any construction and operation would require a separate renewable energy infrastructure licence.

Windlab Chief Development Officer Nathan Blundell said the region’s renewable resources and established industrial sector make it especially compelling for development.

“Whyalla West combines exceptional renewable energy resources, significant development scale and proximity to established and emerging industrial demand,” he said.

Altra Energy Director Andrew Newman said there is an opportunity to power the next generation of industry in the region, which has been heavily impacted by the recent closure of the Whyalla Steelworks.

“The Upper Spencer Gulf has always been a place with a strong industrial history, and this is a chance to power the next generation of that industry,” he said. “We’re already working with major energy users on how this energy will be used.” 

The announcement of the successful tender applicants, comes after the state government earlier this month announced the pipeline of large-scale renewable energy and storage projects under construction or with development approval in South Australia has rocketed in value to more than $32 billion, with almost $7 billion worth of projects already up and running,

South Australia is targeting 100% net renewables by the end of 2027 although Koutsantonis recently hinted the state might not achieve its goal.

“I think we are going to get to 100%. I am confident we can meet that target, but the question for us is going to be is when in 2027 we hit that target” he said during a press conference marking the start of construction on Tilt Renewables’ 288 MW Palmer wind farm 70 kilometres east of Adelaide.

“If we overshoot it a bit, it gets into a little bit of 2028, fine. But the ambition is what’s important. The ambition is what drives the government’s agenda here.”

Government data shows renewables, primarily solar and wind, accounted for 77.1% of the South Australia’s net electricity generation in the 2025 calendar year.

item.title: JV partners flick switch on largest solar farm on NZ’s South Island
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: The largest solar farm on New Zealand’s South Island has been officially opened with joint venture partners Lightsource bp and Contact Energy announcing the launch of the 150 MW Kōwhai Park PV plant.
item.content:encoded:
New Zealand’s solar journey has reached a new milestone with the Kōwhai Park solar farm at Christchurch on the South Island now operational, adding 150 MW of renewable generation capacity to the country’s electricity system.

Developed through New Zealand generator and retailer Contact Energy and Lightsource bp’s joint venture (JV) partnership, the Kōwhai Park solar farm features more than 300,000 panels spread across a 230-hectare site adjacent to and leased from Christchurch Airport.

The 150 MW facility, owned and operated by the JV partners, is expected to generate 275 GWh of renewable energy a year. Long‑term power purchase agreements (PPAs) for the output have been signed with both Christchurch Airport and New Zealand dairy processor Synlait.

Contact Chief Executive Officer Mike Fuge said the $222 million (NZD 273 million) Kōwhai Park project demonstrates the opportunity renewable energy presents for New Zealand. 

“We have huge aspirations for what renewable energy can deliver for this country,” he said. “Building new generation at scale gives businesses the confidence to electrify and strengthens our security of supply. That means a more resilient energy system, with more home-grown generation.”

Lightsource bp Asia-Pacific Chief Operating Officer Adam Pegg said the Kōwhai Park project forms part of the JV partners’ broader efforts to accelerate utility-scale solar deployment across New Zealand. 

“We see significant opportunity for large-scale renewables to support New Zealand’s growing electricity needs, industrial electrification and long-term energy security,” he said. “Kōwhai Park demonstrates the scale of what can be achieved, and we look forward to building on that momentum.”

Kōwhai Park is the first solar project to be completed by the Contact and Lightsource bp JV that was launched in 2022. Other projects in the JV’s development pipeline include a 175 MW solar farm north of Auckland, and a 160 MW solar farm in Taranaki, adjacent to Contact’s Stratford power station.

The launch of the Kōwhai Park solar farm adds to New Zealand’s growing solar portfolio.

A recent report released by the country’s Ministry of Business, Innovation & Employment (MBIE) shows New Zealand’s solar capacity increased by 52% during 2025, reached 830 MW by the end of the year, up from 545 MW at the end of 2024.

The country’s cumulative solar capacity now stands in excess of 1 GW with the 150 MW Tauhei Solar Farm and 38 MW Omeheu Solar Farm also switched on this year.

item.title: Australia leading way to electrification of everything
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: COP31 aims to increase electricity’s share of global final energy demand from 20% to 35% by 2035, accelerating the transition to clean, affordable energy through electrification. Australia is leading with rapid growth in solar, wind, batteries and EVs, demonstrating how renewable energy can lower electricity costs, reduce fossil fuel dependence and support decarbonisation.
item.content:encoded:
The UN Climate Change Conference COP31 will take place in Türkiye in November 2026. A flagship target is to raise the share of final energy demand met by electricity from 20% today to 35% by 2035.

Rising electricity demand signals rising affluence in developing countries, and progress towards “electrification of everything” via solar and wind. Dramatically cheaper, cleaner and more reliable domestic energy is a result.

Most industrial economies (including USA, China, the European Union, Japan and Australia) have annual per capita electricity consumption in the range 6-12 MWh compared with the global average of 4 MWh. For Latin America, India and ASEAN the figure is 1-3 MWh.

In an affluent advanced economy, about 20 MWh of clean electricity per person per year is required for decarbonisation of land transport, heating and cooling in buildings, water heating, and industrial process heat. This is relatively straightforward using off-the-shelf technology.

Another 5-25 MWh per person per year is required for decarbonisation of the chemical industry, which includes metals, plastics, cement, precursor chemicals, and synthetic shipping & aviation fuels. This needs substantial technology development over the next decade.

The “final energy” mentioned in the COP31 target refers to energy products delivered to the consumer, including vehicle fuel, natural gas and electricity. This is a silly measure of energy because it conflates chemical energy with electrical energy. The electricity used in a heat pump or electric vehicle is 3-5 times smaller than fossil fuel energy delivering the same service.

Rapid domestic electrification in Australia

COP31 is led jointly by Türkiye and Australia. Australia has a good electrification story to tell.

Australia is the global No.1 for per capita solar generation, and No.8 for wind. The government target for 2030 is 82% of electricity from renewables (mostly solar and wind), up from 50% today.

The state of South Australia is tracking towards 100% net supply of electricity from solar and wind in 2028. South Australia has become an attractive destination for companies wishing to manufacture using clean energy.

More than 40% of Australian dwellings have rooftop solar (global No.1 per capita), tracking towards 50% by 2030. The average size of new systems is 10 kW with turnkey cost of $10,000. This low cost arises from very smooth government approvals, an experienced workforce, and absence of tariffs.

About 7% of Australian dwellings have home batteries, which is expected to triple by 2030, making Australia the global No.1 per capita. The typical size of new home batteries is 25 kWh. Home battery uptake is driven by government support, which is gradually reducing as it does its job of kick-starting the industry.

A revolution in domestic energy is underway. Home batteries coupled with rooftop solar, heat pumps and an EV allows families to enjoy abundant, clean, reliable and permanently cheap domestic energy: below $800 per year for electricity (and zero natural gas and vehicle fuel bills).

Completion of the 350 GWh Snowy 2.0 system around 2029 will deliver 13 kWh of long duration rechargeable pumped hydro energy storage per person (global No.1).

EV uptake is rising rapidly, driven by the war on Iran. It’s currently at one quarter of new car sales (similar to the global average), although well behind the global leader Norway at 98%.

The rise of solar and batteries is having a remarkable effect on wholesale electricity prices. The graph shows inflation-adjusted average wholesale spot market prices in Australia’s national electricity market since 2012 (blue bars) and the renewable energy fraction of generation (red line). Expensive fossil gas is being pushed out of the market for both ancillary services and peak period power – gas dropped from 13% of generation a decade ago to 3% today.

Authors: Prof. Ricardo Rüther (UFSC) rruther@gmail.com, Prof. Andrew Blakers (ANU) Andrew.blakers@anu.edu.au

ISES, the International Solar Energy Society is a UN-accredited membership NGO founded in 1954 working towards a world with 100% renewable energy for all, used efficiently and wisely.

item.title: Atmos adds BayWa r.e. projects to expanding renewables portfolio
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: Australian clean energy company Atmos Renewables has acquired a portfolio of operating and developing solar and wind projects from BayWa r.e. as the German developer shifts its focus to core European markets.
item.content:encoded:
Atmos Renewables, the renewable energy arm of investment manager Igneo Infrastructure Partners, announced it has taken full ownership of the operating Yatpool and Hughenden solar farms, the advanced Bullawah wind project and a number of earlier stage development projects from BayWa r.e..

Sydney-headquartered Atmos said the acquisition increases its operational portfolio to 19 solar, wind and battery energy storage assets and lifts its operating and in-construction capacity beyond 2 GW, placing it among Australia’s larger renewable energy owner-operators.  

The 106 MW Yatpool Solar Farm is located in northwest Victoria and entered into commercial operation in 2021 with its revenue supported by an offtake arrangement with Australian electricity retailer Flow Power. The asset is about six kilometres from the 112.5 MW Karadoc Solar Farm that Atmos acquired from BayWa r.e. in 2023. 

The 20 MW Hughenden Solar Farm is in central Queensland and has been operating since 2018. The project has a power purchase agreement (PPA) in place with Queensland government-owned gen-tailer CS Energy.  

Atmos has also acquired the Bullawah Wind Farm project proposed for southwest New South Wales (NSW) and several earlier stage developments. The Bullawah project includes plans for up to 800 MW of wind generation alongside a 359 MW two-hour battery but currently only has access rights for a 262 MW wind stage.

Atmos Chief Executive Officer Nigel Baker said together, the projects add further scale and diversity to the company’s growing portfolio.

“This acquisition strengthens our portfolio in two important ways,” he said. “Yatpool and Hughenden add further diversity to our operating portfolio, while the 262 MW Bullawah project positions the company to deliver its first NSW wind farm in the near term, given the advanced state of that project and the REZ access rights it holds.”  

“This allows us to expand the Atmos operating portfolio immediately, while investing in a significant wind project in the NEM region of greatest customer demand.”  

The acquisition follows Atmos’ announcement earlier this month that it had reached financial close on two large-scale projects that will deliver a combined 870 MW of new renewable energy capacity. The projects include the 400 MW / 1,600 MWh Teebar Battery Energy Storage System in Queensland and the 470 MW Parron Maam Marang Farm in Western Australia.

For BayWa, the transaction comes as it presses ahead with a “strategic realignment” revealed earlier this year. In March, the company announced it would turn its focus to “specific core markets” in Europe due to “significantly clouded market conditions” for the renewable energy sector.

BayWa Chief Operating Officer said  Daniel Gäfke the transaction highlights the company’s expertise in identifying, advancing and mitigating risk in large-scale renewable energy developments.

“The successful transfer to Atmos Renewables highlights the strength of high-quality, investment-ready assets and the continued interest in renewable energy infrastructure opportunities,” he said. “We are convinced that these projects will continue to generate significant value under the new owner.”  

Baker said BayWa is now working closely with Atmos to ensure a smooth transition, adding that existing PPAs, landowner agreements and stakeholder commitments will be honoured.

item.title: 1Komma5° announces record investment in AI-based energy management system
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: 1Komma5° has vowed to invest more than $160 million in its energy optimisation platform Heartbeat AI in 2027 as it seeks to expand the capabilities and reach of the energy management system.
item.content:encoded:
Germany-based home energy and electrification company 1Komma5° has announced it will invest more than $160 million (EUR 100 million) in its AI-based energy management system Heartbeat AI next year after raising more than $110 million in its latest financing round.

1Komma5° co-founder and Chief Executive Officer (CEO) Philipp Schröder said the new funds add to the company’s existing investment budget and will support AI development, software capabilities and faster market expansion.

“The objective is clear,” he said. “The energy system needs a universal energy AI that works as an end-to-end operating system. Our ambition is for Heartbeat AI to become exactly that and to bring clean, affordable energy to millions of people.” 

Heartbeat AI is an optimisation layer that connects and controls home energy systems, including solar panels, batteries, heat pumps and electric vehicle chargers. 1Komma5° said the fully automated platform has access to wholesale electricity prices, weather forecasts and grid demand in real time, and automatically decides when to store, use or sell household energy to deliver the best return for customers.

The platform, which is pitched by 1komma5° as an alternative to “conventional” virtual power plant (VPP) programs, is part of the company’s suite of software and hardware products. 1komma5° said it is already compatible with a wide range of energy systems, aggregating more than 1 GW of flexibility capacity in five markets globally, including Australia where the company has attracted more than 60,000 customers since entering the market in 2022.

1Komma5° Australia CEO Luke Stronach said the record investment in Heartbeat AI will enable the continued evolution of the platform, ensuring optimised access to the country’s volatile wholesale electricity market.  

“Wholesale market volatility will continue to be an issue, but Hearbeat AI’s sole focus is on allowing Australian consumers to benefit from this volatility,” he said. “Heartbeat AI is a key element of our vision to deliver the cheapest and cleanest energy possible for everyday Australians.”

1Komma5° said this funding round was led by Japanese cleantech growth fund Marunouchi Innovation Partners (MIP), while existing shareholders including CalSTRS, eCapital, G2 Venture Partners and Eurazeo also participated.

item.title: BloombergNEF forecasts 584 GW of solar installations in 2026
item.dc:creator: David Carroll
item.description: BloombergNEF has cut its 2026 global solar installation forecast to 584 GW, down 10.8% from 2025, driven by a sharper-than-expected slowdown in China. Solar installations outside China are projected to grow to 313 GW, supported by expanding residential and commercial markets.
item.content:encoded:
In December 2025, BloombergNEF projected a pullback in global solar installations, with China slowing and the rest of the world growing. Ten months later, China has slowed more than expected. The rest of the world has grown slightly faster.

BloombergNEF now projects 584 GW of solar installations in 2026. That is a 10.8% decline from 655 GW in 2025. In December, it forecast 649 GW. In the first quarter of 2025, it expected 753 GW. That earlier 2026 figure is 29% higher than today’s forecast.

When asked whether there have been any surprises in the solar industry in 2026 – any Pakistan’s for instance – BloombergNEF CleanTech Analyst Jenny Chase said, “Honestly, none so far, a big theme has been no major booms. I don’t think it has anything to do with Chinese politics or pricing.”

BloombergNEF estimates China installed 383 GW in 2025. It now expects 271 GW in 2026, a 29% decline. In the group’s 2025 Q4 projection, China had been forecast for 2026 was 341 GW.

In December, BloombergNEF CleanTech Analyst Jenny Chase said growth in China “cannot continue at its historical breakneck pace.” She now attributes the deeper slowdown to saturation. “We doubt that either batteries or EVs will halt this, they just slow it down a little,” Chase told pv magazine.

Last year China deployed 383 GW of solar capacity, of which Chase noted the “breakneck” pace. The nation-state is projected to decline a massive 29% to 271 GW deployed. Through the end of June 2026, China installed about 71.8 GW of PV, down from 212.2 GW in the same period of 2025, a even sharper decline of roughly 66%.

The decline came as part of a shift in policy and a  new five year plan taking attention off of capacity, and focusing on energy storage.

Outside of China, non-utility, and batteries

The world has slightly outperformed BloombergNEF’s projections. 2025’s deployment capacity of 272 GW was projected to grow to 308 GW – a 13% pop. Current projections put global capacity at 313 GW deployed, well within the end of 2025’s margin of error.

Growth is coming from markets like India, “chugging along”, the Philippines, Nigeria and Malaysia. Regarding both Nigeria and the Philippines, Chase pointed out that the growth in those markets was almost entirely residential and commercial based.

This aligns with a recent report, shown in the above BloombergNEF chart, that with the pullback in utility scale solar in China – non-utility solar is now the largest sector of global renewable energy investment.

From pv magazine USA

item.title: Valo to deliver 1.6 GWh battery storage system using Wärtsilä GridSolve technology
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: Awarded the contract to deliver the 400 MW / 1,600 MWh Teebar Battery Energy Storage System in Queensland, new energy storage integrator Valo will deploy over 440 containerised batteries for project owner Atmos Renewables.
item.content:encoded:
Born from a joint venture (JV) between Finnish energy tech giant Wärtsilä and German engineering company RCT Solutions GmbH, Valo combines Wärtsilä’s storage technology and software with RCT Solutions’ engineering and manufacturing expertise.

Valo enters the Australian market with over 7.5 GWh across 10 utility-scale energy storage projects in the country, and over 20 GWh globally. It has been selected to deliver for Atmos Renewables the recently announced 400 MW / 1,600 MWh Teebar Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Queensland.

One of the largest battery energy storage system projects currently committed for construction in Queensland, Valo will deploy over 440 containerised batteries using Wärtsilä’s GridSolve Quantum2 technology.

Valo Australia Managing Director Suraj Narayan told pv magazine the GridSolve Quantum2 features just over 4 MW in each enclosure and 444 of them will be delivered to Tee Bar.

“Of course, 1,600 MWh is what we contract to demonstrate during a performance test, but we have more than that in store to plan for calendar degradation, losses in the system, and things like that, so it will be oversized,” Narayan said.

“They are LFP batteries, which is the same technology deployed in all of our projects.”

Teebar is also designed to be a grid forming BESS, the GridSolve Quantum2 batteries will be able to respond quickly to market movements.

“They’re very fast in responding, so grid forming means you don’t have to wait for an external, you can sense the change in frequency and respond to it,” Narayan said.

“More and more grid forming in the future will support more introduction of renewables, which is good.”

Valo will also deploy the GEMS proprietary software at the Teebar project.

“We believe the GEMS software is one of the leading systems in the market. It’s basically intelligent controls and optimisation. GEMS is both a power plant controller (PPC) and energy management system (EMS) in one system, so it’s a complete platform,” Narayan said.

“The advantages are that the software is designed in such a way that it responds quickly, and it talks the same language, whereas if you have two different systems from separate suppliers, for example, this can create issues such as time lags, and response times and things not working properly for flow of information.”

“That shows in our performance in all the projects we’ve done here in Australia or globally, you will never hear of any of our projects getting stuck in commissioning due to delays, and these sorts of things.”

Narayan said a key reason for this is that systems are developed in-house.

“We have a big software team in the United States, and we have local resources to support it, so it’s all in-house knowledge, not a bought in product, and it’s been evolved over the last 15 years and is now in its 8th generation.”

One of the challenges to build the Teebar site, which is located approximately 300 kilometres north of Brisbane in the Fraser Coast region, is remoteness.

“It’s not like building a project close to Newcastle for example, that is close to roads and infrastructure. Tee Bar is a more challenging location; it’s quite far and probably will need upgrades on roads, that sort of thing,” Narayan said.

“And because this 1.6 GWh project requires 440-plus containers of batteries and 130-plus inverters, there will be a lot of transportation, and a lot of trucks have to travel between the port to site, so logistics is a big issue with these projects that needs to be managed properly.”

“Our delivery capability is proven, however. We’ve done a lot of projects in Australia successfully and on time and that experience comes through and it’s these things Atmos has considered when selecting Valo; the delivery capability and the performance of our systems on the grid here.”

Facing a two-year build time until operational, Narayan said there’s still going to be a lot of demand for BESS in the near future, based on the pipeline seen today, and projects that are being planned and forecasts being put out.

“But we are a continent of only 26 million people, so demand for the space will saturate at some point, but there’s a lot of talk about data centres having to bring their own power and if that takes off there could be sustained demand for BESS, otherwise, I believe in the next four or five years demand will start tapering off.”

“As coal steps out there has to be more renewables to replace that and when that happens there’s more variability coming into the grid, so you need more balancing technologies.”

Teebar’s lifescycle is 20 years.

“Atmos develop and hold projects for the long term, which means they have to have a quality project, and I believe that’s one of the reasons they selected Valo because we believe in quality and we’re not the cheapest, but you can rely on our solutions and our design commitments,” Narayan said.

item.title: Large-scale solar sets annual financial investment decision record at 3.5 GW+
item.dc:creator: Ev Foley
item.description: The latest Clean Energy Regulator data shows investment in solar is setting a new annual record with solar final investment decisions for the September 2026 quarter at 1 GW, adding to 3.5 GW already achieved in 2026.
item.content:encoded:
The latest Clean Energy Regulator (CER) data shows investment in solar is setting a new annual record with final investment decisions (FID) for the September quarter sitting at 1 GW, following 2 GW in Q2, adding to the year’s already tallied 3.5 GW, and is approximately 30% above the previous annual solar FID record.

2.1 GW of total large-scale renewable capacity reached FID in the September quarter, which is an equal highest quarterly result, and brings total renewable FID to October 2026 to 5 GW.

That is higher than the previous full-year record of 4.9 GW and brings large-scale FID totals to almost 17 GW since 2022. 

Rooftop solar added 90,042 installations and 894 MW of capacity in the September quarter, which is 35% higher than in Q3 2025, and year-to-date rooftop solar capacity is 45% higher than at the same point in October 2025.

Rooftop solar installations in Q3 were 39% higher than Q3 2025, and has so far added 2.8 GW in 2026, which almost matches the whole of 2025, with three months to go.

Q2 2026 was the biggest rooftop solar capacity quarter on record at 1 GW, and over 13 GW of small-scale solar has been installed since 2022.

Approved capacity under the Cheaper Home Batteries Program (CHBP) reached 15.3 GWh by the end of September, up 1.9 GWh in Q3, and up from less than 2 GWh at the same time in 2025, with total home battery capacity in Australia now more than 5 times greater than when the scheme began on 1 July 2025.  

Cheaper Home Batteries approved capacity has more than tripled during 2026, growing from 5 GWh at the end of 2025 to 15.3 GWh at the end of Q3. With total home battery capacity, including that installed before the scheme, around 19 GWh, it is more than 5 times greater than when the scheme began. 

New South Wales (NSW) has 5.6 GWh of approved home battery capacity, followed by Victoria and Queensland at about 3.2 GWh each.

The data shows about half of approved battery installations are retrofits to existing solar, while about half are going in with new or upgraded rooftop solar.

Federal Minister for Climate Change and Energy Chris Bowen said more renewable energy reaching final investment decision is “what progress looks like”.

“Renewable investment has already broken the annual record with three months still to go. And it isn’t just investment; last month renewable energy generated more electricity in the national grid than fossil fuels,” Bowen said.

“Investors, as well as Australian households and small businesses, are backing Australian renewable energy because they see a government with a clear policy that is working and we’ll continue to get on with the job.”
